```{r hexlogo, echo=FALSE, fig.align="right", out.width="110px", fig.alt="annotatR logo"}
knitr::include_graphics("../man/figures/logo.png")
```

```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 6, fig.height = 4)
library(annotatR)
```

Annotating one image is a job for `at_project()` and the ROI constructors. Annotating a *queue* of images — a plate of serial sections, a batch of slides, a folder of cubes — is what `at_annotate()` is for. It wraps a Shiny app and self-contained HTML5 canvas around a resumable **session**, so you can work through many images without losing your place, your labels, or your unsaved edits.

## Building a session

A session is a queue of image paths plus a shared annotation template. Build one explicitly with `at_session()`, or grab a ready-made one for experimentation with `at_example_session()`, which copies the bundled tissue image into a temporary directory so the queue has real files to iterate.

```{r session}
sess <- at_example_session(3)
sess
```

Every image starts with status `"pending"`, the cursor sits on the first image, and per-image projects are materialised lazily — nothing is read from disk until you visit it.

## Layer templates and label vocabularies

Two things are shared across the whole queue. The **label vocabulary** is the flat list of allowed labels, bound to the number keys `1`–`9`. The **layer template** is a list of `at_layer()` objects — with styles from `at_style()` — stamped onto every image the first time you open it, so each slide starts with the same empty layers ready to receive ROIs.

```{r template}
regions <- at_layer("regions", labels = c("tumour", "necrosis", "stroma"),
                    style = at_style(colour = "#E64B35", fill_alpha = 0.3))
lesions <- at_layer("lesions", labels = c("focus", "margin"),
                    style = at_style(colour = "#4DBBD5", z = 2))

paths <- at_session_status(sess)$path
templated <- at_session(paths,
                        labels = c("tumour", "necrosis", "stroma", "focus", "margin"),
                        layers = list(regions, lesions),
                        out_dir = tempdir())

at_layers(at_current(templated))
```

## Launching the app

With a session in hand, launch the application. This opens a browser and blocks, so it is never run inside a vignette:

```{r launch, eval=FALSE}
at_annotate(templated)
```

`at_annotate()` is forgiving about its first argument: pass a session, a project, an image, a vector of paths, a directory, or `NULL` to open the bundled example.

## Keyboard shortcuts

Tab to a layer or label radio group and use the arrow keys to select it. Tab to
the canvas to draw. Global shortcuts leave text fields, radios, buttons and links
their native behavior; focus the canvas again to use drawing or navigation keys.

| Key | Action |
|-----|--------|
| `n` / `p`, `N` | Next / previous image; next pending image |
| `1`–`9` | Select a label from the active vocabulary |
| `q w e r t y` | Pan, rectangle, polygon, freehand, circle, point |
| Arrows / Shift+arrows | Move the keyboard cursor 1 / 10 level-0 image pixels |
| Enter or Space | Place a point; start/finish a rectangle |
| Space, then Enter | Place polygon vertices, then finish after at least three |
| Escape | Cancel unfinished drawing or editing |
| `d` | Delete the last ROI, if it is unlocked |
| Ctrl+Z / Ctrl+Shift+Z | Undo / redo, respecting locks |
| Shift+Enter | Save synchronously, mark complete and advance after success |
| Shift+V | Copy the previous image's annotations into unlocked target layers |
| `f`, `s`, Ctrl+E, `?` | Flag, save, open Export, shortcut help |

The canvas uses a downsampled image overview (up to 2048 pixels on its longest
side), with pan and zoom. It does not stream pyramid tiles. Drawing coordinates
remain level-0 image pixels. Canvas encoding requires `magick`; TIFF reading can
use `tiff`, but PNG (including the tissue example) needs `magick`. Missing
capabilities and image decoding failures are shown before drawing is enabled.
Navigation remains available when the current image fails.

Layer visibility, color, opacity, stroke width and z-order control display.
Hidden layers do not participate in canvas hit testing. They still participate
in masks and exports: display visibility is not an analytical filter. Locked
layers and imported protected ROIs cannot be edited or removed through the
canvas, keyboard, table or history controls. Adding labels to a locked layer is
also blocked. These protections apply to the app; the R authoring API remains
editable.

## Copy-forward for serial sections

Adjacent serial sections often share most of their anatomy. Rather than redraw it, press `Shift`+`V` to copy ROIs from the previous image into unlocked target layers, then use the edit tool to translate whole regions. Combined with `Shift`+`Enter` (commit and advance), a run of near-identical sections can be annotated in a few keystrokes each.

## Autosave and recovery

By default the app autosaves to `_session.rds` in its `out_dir` after each annotation change. The saved indicator appears only after the checkpoint succeeds. A failed save leaves the current edits marked unsaved and retains the previous valid checkpoint. Press `s` to retry, and resume the last successful checkpoint with `at_resume()`.

New sessions receive distinct temporary output directories. Set an explicit `out_dir` for checkpoints that should survive temporary-directory cleanup. In scripts, `at_save_session()` refuses to replace an existing checkpoint unless you pass `overwrite = TRUE`, including when you omit `path`. App autosave explicitly enables replacement. Loading another folder in the app gives the new queue its own output subdirectory
and retains the previous queue, including unsaved annotations and history.
Use **Data → Restore previous queue** to return after a failed replacement.
This recovery copy lives in the running session: restore and save it before
closing the app. If the replacement queue has unsaved edits, save those entries
before restoring or replacing it again. With `autosave = FALSE`, navigation
retains edits in memory and the indicator stays unsaved until Save succeeds.

```{r resume}
sess <- at_set_status(sess, 1, "complete")
sess <- at_next(sess)

at_save_session(sess)
recovered <- at_resume(file.path(sess$out_dir, "_session.rds"))
recovered
```

The cursor, statuses, materialised projects, and templates all come back intact.

File-backed images persist a versioned descriptor with the canonical source path,
backend and reader options. Pixels are reopened when needed; keep the original
source files available. In-memory images retain their only pixel copy. Session
loading preserves annotation-only projects even when their source is unavailable.

```{r inspect-relink, eval=FALSE}
at_inspect_saved("annotations/_session.rds")
project <- at_current(recovered)
at_inspect_source(project)
project <- at_relink_source(project, "/new/location/original.tif")
recovered$projects[[recovered$cursor]] <- project
at_save_session(recovered, overwrite = TRUE)
```

Relinking explicitly accepts the replacement source after checking image
size, pyramid levels, bands and wavelengths. For readers with non-default options,
pass `options = list(...)` when those options are not present in an old file.
The saved source signature compares file size and modification time. It detects
many replacements but cannot prove content identity, and does not cover sidecar
headers. Changed source metadata requires explicit relinking/revalidation.

Old queue entries without identifiers are migrated by their recorded row position;
existing valid identifiers and geometry are preserved. Legacy lightweight images
can reopen through known default readers, and inspection reports that their reader
options were inferred. Ambiguous identities or unsupported schemas are rejected;
`at_inspect_saved()` reports those issues without modifying the original file.

App checkpoints publish unique complete project files before replacing the session
manifest. Old referenced project files are retained. Unix replacement uses a checked
same-directory rename; Windows replacement uses a previous-file backup and rollback
on an ordinary write failure. These checks do not provide a power-loss durability
guarantee. Do not delete retained files while another checkpoint still refers to them.


## The session API without the app

Everything the canvas does to a session is available as plain functions, which is what makes batches scriptable and testable. Inspect the queue with `at_session_status()`, walk it with `at_next()` / `at_prev()` / `at_goto()`, and read a richer progress report — one column per label — with `at_manifest()`.

```{r api}
at_session_status(sess)

at_manifest(sess)
```

Use these to seed a session programmatically, pre-fill statuses, or audit progress in a report — no Shiny required.

## Export scoping

Ctrl+E opens Export. Choose formats (GeoJSON, QuPath, ROI CSV or mask TIFF)
and scope (current, complete, all or flagged), then activate Export & download.
The app exports all layers of selected annotated projects; it has no layer
selector. Current uses the live project, and other entries use the session's
stored projects. The receipt reports complete files, skips and errors; the ZIP
includes successful artifacts and the receipt. Inspect that receipt before
assuming every requested image and format succeeded.

Those export formats — and how annotatR round-trips with QuPath, GeoJSON, and mask TIFFs — are the subject of the next vignette, "Interoperability".


## Use of LLM tools

Portions of this package were prepared with assistance from large language model tooling for narrowly defined, non-authorial tasks: copyediting, prose smoothing, Markdown/LaTeX formatting, scaffolding of boilerplate files (CI configs, build scripts), code refactoring. The tools used were Chat AI, the LLM service of KISSKI (GWDG), and a self-hosted Mistral Small (24B, Apache-2.0) run locally via Ollama and the ollamar R package — local inference only, with no data sent to third parties for the self-hosted model.
